Vignette: Meena

Meena is a 67-year-old South Asian woman who has been married for over forty years and has spent the better part of her adult life working for a small non-profit that provides legal aid to immigrant families in her city. She is the kind of woman people describe as steady — the one who organizes, who remembers everyone's birthday, who stays late to translate documents for a family that has nowhere else to turn. It is important to understand this about her before understanding what happened, because she understands herself this way too, and the distance between who she was and who she feels herself to be now is one of the things that causes her the most pain.

Fourteen months ago, Meena was sexually assaulted by a colleague — a man she had worked alongside for nearly a decade, someone she had trusted implicitly and defended publicly when others questioned his character. The assault occurred after a fundraising event, in the parking garage of the building where they both worked. She did not report it. She drove home, showered, and the next morning she went back to work. She told no one, not even her husband, Rajiv. In her family, in the community she grew up in, there is no language for what happened to her that does not also become a language of shame. So she swallowed it whole.

For several months she managed, or believed she did. Then the dreams began. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, her heart hammering, the smell of the parking garage — motor oil, cold concrete — so vivid she has to turn on every light in the room. Rajiv has started sleeping in the guest room because her thrashing disturbs him, and she has not told him why, only that she is having "bad sleep." The physical distance between them in the night has become a metaphor for something she cannot name to him.

At work, she has rearranged her entire schedule to avoid the colleague, who remains employed there. She no longer attends staff meetings in person, citing back problems. She takes calls from the lobby rather than her office, which is near his. Her supervisor has noticed she seems distracted, slower to respond to emails, and Meena, who once mentored younger staff with warmth and patience, now closes her door and eats lunch alone. She is acutely aware that her withdrawal is noticed and has constructed careful explanations for all of it. The effort of maintaining those explanations exhausts her.

She startles violently at unexpected sounds — a door slamming, a man's footsteps behind her in a hallway. In grocery stores, she positions herself near exits. She has stopped attending her temple's evening programs, which she had attended every week for thirty years, because the parking lot is poorly lit. Her world has grown systematically smaller, and she experiences this shrinking not as protection but as defeat.

What she describes most painfully is the way she no longer trusts her own judgment. She had trusted him. She had vouched for him. This fact loops through her mind with a relentlessness she cannot interrupt. She finds herself reviewing every professional relationship she has, every person she has believed to be good, and feeling a cold uncertainty settle over all of them. She wonders if she has ever actually known anyone.

She has said nothing to her adult children, who call weekly and ask how she is. She tells them she is tired, which is true, and that work is busy, which is also true. She has become skilled at the partial truth. When her daughter visited last month and said, "Maa, you seem different," Meena smiled and made chai and changed the subject. Later, alone in her kitchen, she stood at the sink for a long time, the water running cold over her hands, and could not remember what she had been about to do.
